matched_rules.because: A cooling failure occurred and the contingency plan called for switching to standby chillers; the standby chillers shared the same water circulation system as the active chillers, so the failover failed.
Mechanical cooling is down and the datacenter is running on its load-dependent thermal buffer; temperatures are rising and approaching safe operational thresholds.
Data center temperatures are increasing and cooling capacity is insufficient; the data center is at risk of exceeding safe operating temperatures.
Cooling system has failed and server room temperatures are rising uncontrollably; temperatures are approaching the level that could trigger the fire sprinkler system.
Chillers have been recirculated and gas discharged but will not restart; the site's chillers are configured as a bound cluster.
Chillers have tripped offline and are being manually restarted; the chilled-water loop serving those chillers has been sitting without cooling.
Chillers supporting a data hall have tripped offline; the data hall requires a minimum number of operational chillers to stay within thermal thresholds.
Chillers cannot be restarted because the chilled-water loop is too hot; data hall temperatures are continuing to increase.
A voltage event has tripped multiple chillers and manual restart is required; the Chiller Management System has not yet been changed to prevent restart failures.

next_actions.action: Immediately verify that mechanical cooling systems are still running, rather than assuming surge suppressors protected them; if mechanical cooling has shut down, treat the datacenter as being on a load-dependent thermal buffer and start planning for its depletion; transfer the rest of the datacenter to generators to stabilize the power supply while storms are still active.

Treat the thermal buffer as a finite resource and act before it is depleted; expect that once the buffer is gone, temperature will exceed safe operational thresholds and automated device shutdown will begin; recognize that in parts of the datacenter temperature can rise so quickly that hardware is damaged before it can shut down.

Do not assume standby chillers will take over; confirm the standby plant draws from an independent water circuit before relying on it; if the standby shares the same water loop, treat the failover as likely to fail and move directly to auxiliary heat dissipation and ventilation measures; notify the chiller manufacturer early rather than waiting for the failover to prove ineffective.

Progressively decrease the thermal load within the data center space; consider terminating non-critical workloads such as Preemptible VMs to reduce thermal load and ensure space for zonal failover activities; if thermal load reduction is insufficient, power down servers to prevent an even longer outage and further impact to infrastructure.

Begin reducing loads on computing, storage, network, database, and big data clusters to slow temperature rise; shut down servers in rooms with high temperature; treat sprinkler activation as a risk that can damage power supply cabinets and server racks and complicate restoration.

Recognize that individual chiller restart will not work while the chillers remain bound into a cluster; plan to manually modify chiller configurations to unbind them from the cluster so each can be restarted individually; expect that restarting chillers one after another will slow restoration of the whole cooling system.

Recognize that once loop water reaches elevated temperatures the chiller self-protection mechanism will inhibit restart to prevent damage; prioritize restarting the chillers that serve the most thermally exposed data halls before the loop heats past the restart limit; if restart is inhibited, plan to reduce the thermal load so the loop can cool, rather than repeatedly attempting restart.

Count how many chillers each impacted data hall still has running against its minimum requirement; treat any data hall below its minimum as being in thermal runaway risk and act on load before temperatures climb; account for standby chillers separately from running chillers when judging margin.

Reduce the thermal load by shutting down networking, compute, and storage infrastructure in the impacted data halls; treat this shutdown as the means to bring the chilled-water loop back to a safe temperature so chillers can be restarted; accept the loss of service availability in the affected zone as the cost of protecting data durability and infrastructure health.

Increase technician staffing at the datacenter so manual restart procedures can be executed promptly; assign teams so restarts can proceed in parallel across data halls rather than sequentially; treat staffing as a temporary mitigation until the control timing logic change is in place.

escalate.reason: Thermal buffer depletion is imminent or automated shutdowns have started; simultaneous failure of redundant cooling systems and rising temperatures; temperatures continue to rise despite initial load reduction; chillers remain blocked from restart by high loop temperature.

not_covered: No rule addresses the specific scenario of chiller malfunction due to air entering the cooling system from lack of water, which is the root cause here.
No rule covers the situation where the chiller manufacturer is notified but the issue remains unsolved after multiple attempts.
No rule addresses the coordination with the data center infrastructure provider's engineers for manual isolation and restoration of chillers.

per_finding.note: The triage does not mention air entering the cooling system due to lack of water as the root cause.
R-007 explicitly warns that standby chillers may share the same water circuit and failover will fail.
R-008 states individual chiller restart will not work while chillers are bound into a cluster and calls for unbinding.
R-006 and R-009 direct reducing loads on computing, storage, network, database, and big data clusters to slow temperature rise.
R-008 directs manually modifying chiller configurations to unbind them from the cluster so each can be restarted individually.
R-009 treats sprinkler activation as a risk that can damage power supply cabinets and server racks and complicate restoration.
R-007 already applies the practice of confirming standby plant independence and not assuming failover will work.
The triage already applies standardized load-reduction and shutdown actions, though it does not explicitly call for a contingency plan update.
No rule in the triage addresses expanding monitoring metrics or improving troubleshooting efficiency.
